mainEntity.name: How much does it cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the result you want, and we agree it privately after the first conversation. There is no retainer and no published price.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to be technical?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. That is rather the point. We handle the technical side, and everything the system shows you is in plain English.

mainEntity.name: What happens when the work ends?

acceptedAnswer.text: It keeps running. You own the system, the automations and the record of your standards, and nothing about it depends on us being there.

mainEntity.name: Who sees my data?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mindmake and the providers needed to run the service. After email confirmation, you receive the brief and our team receives a fit summary. We do not sell or publish your information. Full details are in our privacy policy.

mainEntity.name: Does anyone in my company need to know?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The work happens on your own decisions, with you, and nobody else in the business has to be told you started. Where the work needs your team, you decide when and how they come in.

mainEntity.name: How is this different from hiring a consultant?

acceptedAnswer.text: A consultant does good work and then the project closes. We build the system inside your accounts, so what it learns about your work is still there next year.

mainEntity.name: Can I not just use ChatGPT?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can, and you should. Those tools are excellent. They just start from nothing every morning. The brain is the part that remembers your standards, so the tools you already pay for start from you.

mainEntity.name: Where do I use my AI brain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wherever the work is that you want to speed up, hand off or do better. During the build we choose with you which tools to chain together for it, build your Brain into them and prove it on real work. It belongs to you, and no single AI company holds it.

mainEntity.name: How do I keep my AI brain up to date?

acceptedAnswer.text: You tell it what changed, in plain words and without code, and the work built on that standard follows. Before we finish, we show you how to run each tool we built, so nothing waits on us.

mainEntity.name: How much of my team's time does this take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Very little of it. We need your decisions, the context you trust and a few introductions. There is no homework and no all-team rollout to sit through.

mainEntity.name: What do we keep at the end?

acceptedAnswer.text: The system, the automations and the record of your standards. All of it is yours, and it keeps working after we finish.

mainEntity.name: Do I get a document or something that works?

acceptedAnswer.text: Something that works, plus the evidence behind it. You can see every source we used and check the reasoning yourself.

mainEntity.name: How soon do I see something working?

acceptedAnswer.text: In the first week. We take on one result rather than a whole transformation, so the first working piece goes live early and it improves each week after that.

mainEntity.name: How do I start?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start here, at the top or bottom of any page. You give us four details: your first name, your last name, your work email and the part of the business you work in. We read your company from the email, so there is nothing to look up, and a plan built for your business lands in your inbox.

mainEntity.name: Is this a fit for my business?

acceptedAnswer.text: It suits a leader who owns the decision and wants one real result, proved on real work. If that is not you yet, the weekly read is a good place to begin.

mainEntity.name: Will you email me forever?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two emails, ever. Your results, and one follow-up two weeks later. Nothing else, and no drip sequence. If you ask us to email your brief we send a six-digit code first, so we know the address is yours.

mainEntity.name: What actually happens in the work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Week one we learn how you decide, from real work rather than a questionnaire. Week two the first piece goes live and you use it. After that we connect it to the tools your week already runs on and tighten it against what you actually did with it. You see something working from the first week, not a plan at the end.

mainEntity.name: What is included?

acceptedAnswer.text: The working system inside your own accounts, the automations around it, the written record of your standards, and the evidence behind every recommendation. You also get the reasoning, so you can check it rather than take our word for it.

mainEntity.name: Why do I need this? Could I not do it myself?

acceptedAnswer.text: You could, and some people should. What usually stops it is not capability, it is that the work never reaches the top of anyone's week. We bring the time, the tooling and the pattern from having done it before, and we leave you owning it rather than depending on us.

mainEntity.name: How do you charge?

acceptedAnswer.text: On the result, agreed before we start, and not on hours or a monthly retainer. We say what the work will produce, you agree the number privately, and it does not move afterwards. There is nothing to cancel at the end because there is nothing running.

mainEntity.name: What if it does not work?

acceptedAnswer.text: You would know inside the first week rather than at the end, because something real is running by then. If it is clearly not going to be worth it we say so and stop, and you keep whatever has been built up to that point.

mainEntity.name: We tried AI and it got things wrong. Why would this be different?

acceptedAnswer.text: It will get things wrong, and so will the next one. What matters is what happens then. Writing, the loom, the calculator and satnav all drew the same objection when they first slipped, and the objection was rarely about accuracy. A system built inside your own accounts, that shows its sources and says when it cannot know, is one you can check rather than one you have to trust.

acceptedAnswer.text: No. What matters is that one person can decide, and that there is real work to point it at. It has been useful to a solo practice and to a publisher with a few hundred people, for the same reason both times.

@graph.headline: What is a data company worth when AI can do the analysis?
@graph.description: When a buyer's own AI can analyse anything, a data company has to sell rights, a place in the decision and judgement, and change how it prices and sells.
@graph.abstract: A data company keeps its value by selling what a buyer's AI cannot make for itself: data with clear rights and a known source, a place inside the customer's decisions, and the judgement to say what the numbers mean for that customer. When analysis gets cheap, the price has to follow the decision the data improves rather than the report, and the way the company sells has to change with it.

about.name: how does a data company stay valuable when AI can do the analysis

mainEntity.name: Is our data still a moat?

acceptedAnswer.text: Partly. Data that is exclusive, cleanly licensed and kept fresh is hard to copy. Data anyone can gather, or that a buyer's AI can estimate well enough, is not a moat however large it is.

mainEntity.name: Should we sell our data to AI companies?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be a real line of revenue, and it can also train a competitor. Decide which data you would sell, on what terms and at what price before a buyer asks, so the deal fits a plan you already have.

mainEntity.name: What changes for the sales team?

acceptedAnswer.text: They sell the decision the data improves and the proof that it improved. That usually means new questions when they first meet a buyer, new proof in the pitch, and often a different person to sell to.

@graph.description: Correcting AI in the moment fixes one answer. Recording the correction and its reason fixes every answer after it. Here is how that works.
@graph.abstract: An AI system gets better at a particular business's work when each correction is recorded with its reason and kept alongside the earlier view, so the next answer starts from the corrected position. Correcting an AI in the middle of a conversation fixes that one answer and is lost when the conversation ends. A kept record of corrections turns everyday edits into lasting improvements that people can see, check and reverse.

about.name: how do I make an AI system learn from our corrections over time

mainEntity.name: Is this the same as fine-tuning a model?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Fine-tuning changes the model itself, which is slow, costly and hard to inspect. A correction record sits beside the model and is read before each answer, so it can be seen, edited and reversed by a person.

mainEntity.name: Why keep the earlier view?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the reason something changed is part of the judgement. Keeping the earlier view shows what was believed, what changed and why, which stops the same mistake being made again by someone who never saw it.

mainEntity.name: Who makes the corrections?

acceptedAnswer.text: The people whose judgement the system is meant to carry. Usually a leader and a few senior colleagues, correcting real outputs as part of their normal work.

about.name: what decisions should humans still make when AI can do most of the work

mainEntity.name: Does a person need to check every AI output?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Checking everything turns review into a rubber stamp. Check what reaches customers, what cannot be undone and what defines the standard. Sample the rest.

mainEntity.name: What counts as reaching the outside world?

acceptedAnswer.text: Anything a customer, partner, investor or regulator will see or rely on. Emails sent, prices quoted, contracts signed, public posts and published figures.

mainEntity.name: Will the line move over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and it should. As a team gains evidence that a kind of work is reliable, it can move that work to the delegated side. Record the change and the reason, so the next person understands it.

mainEntity.name: How long before it is useful?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is useful on the first real decision it is given, because even a small record of past reasoning beats none. It gets more useful with every decision and correction added afterwards.

@graph.headline: An AI decision tool earns trust by holding your judgement, not by passing an audit
@graph.description: Governance tells a leadership team that a tool was built carefully. It cannot tell them it is right for this business. Trust is a question about memory.
@graph.abstract: An AI decision tool is trustworthy enough for a leadership team when it can show which of that team's own standards and past decisions shaped an answer, and when a person can follow that trail back and argue with it. Governance checks such as documented testing, audit logs and a named human owner tell you the tool was built carefully, and they say nothing about whether its advice fits this business. The test that separates the two is a replay: the tool is given a decision the team has already made, with the outcome hidden, and its reasoning is compared with the reasoning the team actually used.

about.name: how do I evaluate whether an AI decision tool is trustworthy enough for my leadership team

mainEntity.name: Is a governance framework enough on its own?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is enough for the questions a regulator, an insurer or a board committee will ask, and being able to answer those is worth having. It says nothing about whether a recommendation fits the business it was made for, because nothing in a risk framework asks what this leadership team has already decided.

mainEntity.name: What counts as a record of a leadership team's judgement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decisions the team has already made, the reasons behind them, the standards they hold and the constraints they work inside, written down in a form a system can read. Most of it exists already, scattered through board papers, pricing exceptions, memos and the arguments that ended a plan early.

mainEntity.name: What if the tool cannot show where an answer came from?

acceptedAnswer.text: Then the only way to check it is to already know the answer, which removes the reason for having it. A tool that cannot be checked is one the most senior person in the room has to take on faith, and faith is not a control.

mainEntity.name: Does this apply to the general assistants a team already uses?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and it is where the gap shows first. A general assistant is trained on the public record and knows nothing about the last three decisions this team made, which makes it a fast writer and an average adviser.

about.name: how to build an AI center of excellence without a dedicated engineering budget

mainEntity.name: Can one person run an AI Center of Excellence alone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the function is treated as governance and standards rather than a build team. The three real jobs, deciding what good use looks like, catching bad use early, and retaining what's learned, don't require engineers, they require a system that holds the standard and gets checked before decisions get made.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between a CoE and an AI governance policy document?

acceptedAnswer.text: A policy document is written once and gets forgotten. A CoE, even a one-person one, has to be a running function that gets consulted before decisions happen, not a reference that people are supposed to remember to check.

mainEntity.name: When does an AI CoE actually need dedicated engineers?

acceptedAnswer.text: When the standards need to be enforced automatically across large volumes of output, or when the organisation is building its own AI tools rather than governing the use of existing ones. Most leaders asking this question are doing the latter.

mainEntity.name: What should the first thing a leader builds be, if not a team?

acceptedAnswer.text: A running system that encodes what good AI-assisted decisions look like in the two or three areas where a bad call actually costs something, and that gets checked before, not after, the decision is made.

about.name: how do I calculate the total addressable revenue opportunity for AI products in publishing

mainEntity.name: What inputs do I need before I can size an AI product's revenue opportunity?

acceptedAnswer.text: Current subscriber count and churn rate, blended ad RPM and monthly sessions, the value of recent licensing deals in your tier, and the fully loaded cost of running the product. All four sit in finance and ad ops, not in a market report.

mainEntity.name: Is a TAM/SAM/SOM report useless for this decision?

acceptedAnswer.text: A TAM/SAM/SOM report answers how big the category is. It cannot tell you what your specific subscriber base, ad stack or licensing book is worth, because it was never built from your data.
